quote: Dann wäre wahrscheinlich (wie durch [-...-] Multiplication mit der conjugirten Wurzel folgt) zugleich die Diophantische Gl. $g_1^2-(x^2-1)g_2^2=1$ oder $X^2-(x^2-1)Y^2=1$ gelöst.
english: Then probably (as follows by multiplication with the conjugate root) the Diophantine equation g_1^2-(x^2-1)g_2^2=1, or X^2-(x^2-1)Y^2=1, would be solved at the same time.
topic: Notes on continued-fraction and rational approximation of logarithms of algebraic functions (linked to the Pell-type equation $X^2-(x^2-1)Y^2=1$), simultaneous rational approximation of two functions, and using solutions of first-order linear differential equations as test cases for proving irrationality of function values.

triage.modern_statement: In C[x], find all polynomial solutions (X, Y) of the polynomial Pell equation X^2 - (x^2-1) Y^2 = 1. Hilbert's remark ties this to rational approximation of log(x+sqrt(x^2-1)) = arccosh x. If g1 + g2*sqrt(x^2-1) were an exact unit, then multiplying it by its conjugate g1 - g2*sqrt(x^2-1) would give g1^2 - (x^2-1) g2^2 = 1. In modern terms this is the classical Abel–Chebyshev link: an integral of the form ∫ρ/√D dx can be written as a logarithm, log((P+Q√D)/(P−Q√D)), exactly when the polynomial Pell equation P^2 − D Q^2 = const ≠ 0 has a nontrivial solution. That in turn happens exactly when the continued fraction of √D in C((1/x)) is periodic.
triage.answered_by: This was already classical before Hilbert. Abel (1826) proved the equivalence between logarithmic integrability, polynomial Pell solvability and periodic continued fractions of √D, and Chebyshev (1852) studied it again. For the specific case D = x^2 − 1 the complete solution is given by the Chebyshev polynomials: (x+√(x^2−1))^n = T_n(x) + U_{n−1}(x)√(x^2−1), so T_n^2 − (x^2−1)U_{n−1}^2 = 1. Modern work on the general polynomial Pell equation includes Zannier and coauthors, e.g. arXiv:1602.00934.

evidence.claim: Abel in 1826, and Chebyshev in 1852, studied the continued fraction expansion of the square root of a complex polynomial D(t).

Abel and Chebyshev first developed continued fractions of quadratic irrationalities in function fields to express hyperelliptic integrals in finite terms. Abel's theorem links such an integral to a solution (p,q) of the Pell equation for D.
Abel (1826) gave the criterion for when ∫ρ dx/√R is a logarithm of an expression in R and polynomials, i.e. the genesis of the polynomial Pell / logarithmic integral connection.

The polynomial Pell equation was first studied in connection with integrating certain algebraic functions in elementary terms (Abel, 1826), and its solvability is equivalent to periodicity of the continued fraction.
Wikipedia's article on Pell's equation notes the connection between Pell's equation and the Chebyshev polynomials, which are exactly the polynomial solutions for D = x^2 − 1.

triage.why: The equation in the note, X^2 − (x^2−1)Y^2 = 1, has well-known polynomial solutions: the Chebyshev pairs (T_n, U_{n−1}). These come from expanding (x+√(x^2−1))^n; that identity is standard and does not depend on the search results. The link Hilbert suspected, between rational/continued-fraction approximation of the logarithm of an algebraic function and solving the Pell equation 'by multiplication with the conjugate root', is Abel's 1826 theorem, later developed by Chebyshev. So the conjecture as written is classically true and is not one of Hilbert's published problems. The general polynomial Pell equation, together with continued fractions in function fields and their links to Jacobians and torsion points, is still actively researched (arXiv 2016–2017 papers). Confidence is medium rather than high because the page is fragmentary: it is not certain which exact approximation Hilbert meant (log(x+√(x^2−1)) is my reading). No source discusses this notebook entry directly.
